annotations.text: Best-of-N sampling improves code generation but requires execution for candidate selection. Entropy dynamics (EDIS) have shown promise for detecting reasoning errors in math problems by identifying instability patterns in per-token entropy trajectories. We test whether entropy dynamics can provide execution-free selection signals for code generation by adapting EDIS as nEDIS with pre-registered success criteria. Our experiments demonstrate a clear negative result: nEDIS fails the pre-registered criterion, underperforming even random first-sample selection by 12.8–27.5 percentage points on HumanEval and MBPP. We identify entropy sparsity as a key failure mode—88.3% of entropy values are exactly zero with instruction-tuned code models, undermining spike detection. The optimization required to improve nEDIS contradicts the original hypothesis, suggesting the method captures length bias rather than meaningful entropy dynamics. This negative result prevents wasted effort and suggests alternative approaches are needed for execution-free code selection.
annotations.comment:
This abstract is well-structured for a negative-result paper, following a clean arc: problem -> prior method -> adaptation -> negative finding -> failure mode -> implication.

**Concrete issue:** The abstract claims that "the optimization required to improve nEDIS contradicts the original hypothesis," but it does not specify what this optimization entailed (inverting selection direction from argmin to argmax and multiplying by length T). Without this brief specification, the claim of contradiction remains vague and hard to assess from the abstract alone.

**Why it matters:** Readers need to understand exactly what changed to judge whether the contradiction is genuine or merely a post-hoc rationalization. For a negative result paper, the specific mechanics of the failed adaptation are a core contribution.

**Revision requirement:** Add one clause briefly describing the optimization (argmax + length multiplication) and its semantic shift.

Mentor Revised Version:
Best-of-N sampling improves code generation but requires execution for candidate selection. Entropy dynamics (EDIS) have shown promise for detecting reasoning errors in math problems by identifying instability patterns in per-token entropy trajectories. We test whether entropy dynamics can provide execution-free selection signals for code generation by adapting EDIS as nEDIS with pre-registered success criteria. Our experiments demonstrate a clear negative result: nEDIS fails the pre-registered criterion, underperforming even random first-sample selection by 12.8–27.5 percentage points on HumanEval and MBPP. We identify entropy sparsity as a key failure mode—88.3% of entropy values are exactly zero with instruction-tuned code models, undermining spike detection. The post-hoc optimization required to improve nEDIS (inverting selection to argmax and multiplying by sequence length) contradicts the original low-instability hypothesis, suggesting the method captures length bias rather than meaningful entropy dynamics. This negative result prevents wasted effort and suggests alternative approaches are needed for execution-free code selection.
annotations.summary: Abstract is well-structured for a negative result, but the 'contradiction' claim needs one clause explaining what the optimization actually was.

annotations.text: Best-of-N sampling has emerged as a simple yet effective technique for improving code generation quality (Chen et al., 2021). By generating multiple candidate solutions and selecting the best one, this approach can substantially improve pass@1 accuracy over greedy decoding. However, selecting the best candidate typically requires executing code against test cases—a process that is slow, requires test availability, and poses security risks when running untrusted code. Execution-free selection methods would enable faster inference and broader applicability, but developing reliable selection signals without execution remains an open challenge.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph establishes the practical motivation for execution-free code selection: Best-of-N improves quality but requires test execution, which is slow and risky.

**Concrete issue:** The paragraph is clear and well-motivated, but it does not quantify how much Best-of-N improves over greedy decoding, or how costly execution is in practice. Adding one concrete number (e.g., typical Best-of-N gain or execution overhead) would strengthen the stakes significantly.

**Why it matters:** Without quantitative stakes, the reader may not appreciate the real-world importance of execution-free selection. Negative result papers benefit from clearly motivating why the tested hypothesis mattered enough to be worth testing.

**Revision requirement:** Add one sentence quantifying Best-of-N gain over greedy and/or execution overhead.

Mentor Revised Version:
Best-of-N sampling has emerged as a simple yet effective technique for improving code generation quality (Chen et al., 2021). By generating multiple candidate solutions and selecting the best one, this approach can improve pass@1 accuracy by 5–15 percentage points over greedy decoding on standard benchmarks. However, selecting the best candidate typically requires executing code against test cases—a process that is slow (minutes per problem), requires test availability, and poses security risks when running untrusted code. Execution-free selection methods would enable faster inference and broader applicability, but developing reliable selection signals without execution remains an open challenge.
annotations.summary: Motivation paragraph is clear but lacks quantitative stakes; add one sentence on Best-of-N gain or execution overhead.

annotations.text: Recent work on entropy dynamics offers a promising direction. EDIS (Entropy Dynamics Instability Score) (Zhu et al., 2026) demonstrated that per-token entropy trajectories during generation can diagnose reasoning errors in mathematical problem-solving. The key insight is that incorrect reasoning exhibits characteristic instability patterns—“burst spikes” of sustained entropy increase and “rebound spikes” of sharp entropy recovery after false confidence. These patterns distinguish correct from incorrect solutions without requiring ground-truth labels, suggesting that generation uncertainty dynamics might provide useful signals about output quality.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph introduces EDIS and its core mechanism: burst spikes and rebound spikes in per-token entropy trajectories diagnose reasoning errors in math.

**Concrete issue:** The paragraph accurately summarizes the EDIS intuition but does not critically examine why entropy dynamics might work differently for code vs math. Code generation with instruction-tuned models is typically highly structured and confident, whereas math reasoning involves exploratory steps with genuine uncertainty. This fundamental distributional difference is crucial context that should be flagged before testing the transfer hypothesis.

**Why it matters:** Without this contrast, the later discovery of 88.3% entropy sparsity appears as an after-the-fact surprise rather than an expected consequence of differing generation dynamics. A stronger introduction would anticipate this mode mismatch.

**Revision requirement:** Add one sentence contrasting the entropy distribution characteristics of code vs math generation.

Mentor Revised Version:
Recent work on entropy dynamics offers a promising direction. EDIS (Entropy Dynamics Instability Score) (Zhu et al., 2026) demonstrated that per-token entropy trajectories during generation can diagnose reasoning errors in mathematical problem-solving. The key insight is that incorrect reasoning exhibits characteristic instability patterns—"burst spikes" of sustained entropy increase and "rebound spikes" of sharp entropy recovery after false confidence. These patterns distinguish correct from incorrect solutions without requiring ground-truth labels, suggesting that generation uncertainty dynamics might provide useful signals about output quality. However, code generation with instruction-tuned models typically produces highly confident, structured outputs, which may differ fundamentally from the exploratory uncertainty patterns observed in mathematical reasoning.
annotations.summary: EDIS summary is accurate but misses the expected distributional difference between code (confident, structured) and math (exploratory, uncertain) generation.

annotations.text: This naturally raises the question: can entropy dynamics guide execution-free code selection? We hypothesize that similar instability patterns might indicate unreliable code generation, enabling selection of correct candidates without execution. To test this hypothesis rigorously, we adapt EDIS to code generation as nEDIS (Normalized EDIS), introducing length and scale normalizations appropriate for variable-length code. We pre-register a success criterion: nEDIS must significantly outperform both confound baselines (length-only selection and entropy coefficient of variation) on both benchmarks (HumanEval and MBPP) to demonstrate that spike-structure provides selection signal beyond simple confounds.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the hypothesis and the nEDIS adaptation with pre-registered success criteria.

**Concrete issue:** The pre-registered success criterion is methodologically sound—requiring nEDIS to beat both confound baselines on both benchmarks. However, the paragraph does not discuss why the chosen confounds (Length-only and CV_H) are sufficient to isolate spike-structure signal. For instance, one could argue that Mean_H or Self-Certainty are equally important confounds. This leaves a potential p-hacking concern: if nEDIS beats some baselines but not others, could the criterion be redefined post-hoc?

**Why it matters:** For a negative result paper, the rigor of the success criterion is a key strength. Making the confound choice explicit strengthens defensibility against accusations of cherry-picked baselines.

**Revision requirement:** Add one sentence justifying why Length-only and CV_H are the primary confounds to test against.

Mentor Revised Version:
This naturally raises the question: can entropy dynamics guide execution-free code selection? We hypothesize that similar instability patterns might indicate unreliable code generation, enabling selection of correct candidates without execution. To test this hypothesis rigorously, we adapt EDIS to code generation as nEDIS (Normalized EDIS), introducing length and scale normalizations appropriate for variable-length code. We pre-register a success criterion: nEDIS must significantly outperform both confound baselines (length-only selection and entropy coefficient of variation) on both benchmarks (HumanEval and MBPP). These confounds are chosen because length is the most obvious proxy for code quality (longer code may be more complete), and CV_H isolates entropy variability without the spike-detection mechanism. Outperforming both demonstrates that spike-structure provides selection signal beyond simple confounds.
annotations.summary: Pre-registered criterion is sound but lacks brief justification for why Length-only and CV_H were selected as the primary confounds.

annotations.text: Our experiments yield a clear negative result. nEDIS fails the pre-registered criterion: while it beats the CV H baseline on both benchmarks, it fails to beat length-only selection on MBPP (41.5% vs 66.4%, p = 1.0). More critically, all entropy-based methods—including the optimized nEDIS v2—underperform trivial baselines. Random first-sample selection achieves 68.9%/69.0% on HumanEval/MBPP, while nEDIS v2 achieves only 56.1%/41.5%. We identify a key failure mode: 88.3% of per-token entropy values are exactly zero due to high model confidence, making spike detection inherently noisy and unreliable for code generation with instruction-tuned models.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph summarizes the main experimental findings and previews the contributions.

**Concrete issue:** The statement that nEDIS "fails to beat length-only selection on MBPP (41.5% vs 66.4%, p = 1.0)" is technically correct but potentially confusing. A p-value of 1.0 in a one-sided test where the delta is -24.9pp means the one-sided test is testing H1: nEDIS v2 > Length-only, and the result is so strongly in the opposite direction that p is reported as 1.0. This phrasing may mislead readers who interpret p=1.0 as "no difference" rather than "strongly worse."

**Why it matters:** For a negative result paper, precise statistical communication is essential. A p=1.0 could be misconstrued as statistical non-significance (no direction) rather than strong evidence in the wrong direction.

**Revision requirement:** Clarify that p=1.0 reflects a one-sided test where nEDIS v2 is significantly worse than Length-only on MBPP.

More critically, all entropy-based methods—including the optimized nEDIS v2—underperform trivial baselines. Random first-sample selection achieves 68.9%/69.0% on HumanEval/MBPP, while nEDIS v2 achieves only 56.1%/41.5%. We identify a key failure mode: 88.3% of per-token entropy values are exactly zero due to high model confidence, making spike detection inherently noisy and unreliable for code generation with instruction-tuned models.

annotations.text:
Our contributions are:
• We provide a rigorous negative result showing that entropy dynamics do not transfer from math reasoning to code generation, with pre-registered success criteria and statistical significance testing.
• We identify entropy sparsity as a fundamental failure mode: instruction-tuned code models are highly confident on most tokens, undermining the spike-detection mechanism that EDIS relies on.
• We release our code and data to prevent others from pursuing this direction and to enable future research on alternative execution-free selection methods.
annotations.comment:
This section lists three contribution claims for the paper.

**Concrete issue:** The contributions are well-articulated for a negative result paper, but contribution C3 ("We release our code and data to prevent others from pursuing this direction") frames code release as a primary scientific contribution. While code release is valuable for reproducibility, it is not typically classified as a core scientific contribution. This risks weakening the perceived research value of the paper by diluting substantive claims with engineering practices.

**Why it matters:** In peer review, code release is considered a best practice rather than a novel intellectual contribution. Overstating it as a contribution may reduce the weight given to C1 and C2. A stronger framing would emphasize the methodological insight (entropy sparsity as a failure mode) and the rigorous negative-result protocol (pre-registered criteria).

**Revision requirement:** Reframe C3 to emphasize community impact or methodological guidance rather than code release alone.

Mentor Revised Version:
Our contributions are:

• We provide a rigorous negative result showing that entropy dynamics do not transfer from math reasoning to code generation, validated with pre-registered success criteria and statistical significance testing.

• We identify entropy sparsity as a fundamental failure mode: instruction-tuned code models are highly confident on most tokens (88.3% zero entropy), undermining the spike-detection mechanism that EDIS relies on. This insight explains why token-level entropy dynamics are structurally mismatched for code generation.

• We establish a reproducible template for negative-result evaluation in execution-free code selection, including our pre-registered success criterion, benchmarking protocol, and publicly released code. This prevents redundant effort and provides a foundation for future research on alternative approaches.
annotations.summary: Contribution C3 frames code release as a core scientific contribution, which may dilute perceived research value; reframe to emphasize methodological guidance.

annotations.text: Execution-Free Code Selection. Several approaches have been proposed for selecting code without execution. Top-Pass (Lyu et al., 2024) trains a ranker to maximize pass@k by learning from execution feedback, achieving significant improvements but requiring training data with execution labels. Zhu et al. (2025) use uncertainty-guided chain-of-thought to improve code generation. Valentin et al. (2025) propose incoherence as an oracle-less measure of error, detecting inconsistencies across multiple generations. Unlike these approaches, we test whether entropy dynamics alone can provide selection signals without any training or execution feedback.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph surveys execution-free code selection methods, mentioning Top-Pass, uncertainty-guided CoT, and incoherence measures.

**Concrete issue:** The related work omits several highly relevant recent papers that directly address entropy-based or uncertainty-based evaluation for code generation. For instance:
- Sharma & David (2025) show that token-level entropy fails to correlate with code correctness unless adapted with symbolic execution-based semantic clustering [1].
- Yang et al. (2024) demonstrate that LLM entropy effectively measures code "unnaturalness" for Automated Program Repair, achieving 50% improvements in fault localization [2].
- Ribeiro et al. (2025) find that output probabilities are poorly correlated with code correctness and propose internal representation-based selection that outperforms log-likelihood ranking [3].
- Bouchard et al. (2026) evaluate token-probability-based UQ methods for code, finding mixed results and proposing functional entropy as a superior alternative [4].

**Why it matters:** Omitting these works significantly weakens the novelty positioning. The manuscript claims to test whether entropy dynamics provide selection signals, but prior work has already found that raw token-level entropy is unreliable for code correctness [1, 3] and requires code-specific adaptations [1, 4]. The EDIS negative result is consistent with these prior findings, which should be acknowledged and positioned as complementary evidence rather than ignored.

**Revision requirement:** Add a paragraph or expand the existing one to cover these works, explicitly stating how the current negative result aligns with and extends these prior findings on the limitations of token-level entropy for code.

References:
[1] Assessing Correctness in LLM-Based Code Generation via Uncertainty Estimation 2502.11620

[2] Revisiting Unnaturalness for Automated Program Repair in the Era of Large Language Models 2404.15236

[3] On LLMs' Internal Representation of Code Correctness 2512.07404

[4] Functional Entropy: Predicting Functional Correctness in LLM-Generated Code with Uncertainty Quantification 2605.28500

Mentor Revised Version:
Execution-Free Code Selection. Several approaches have been proposed for selecting code without execution. Top-Pass (Lyu et al., 2024) trains a ranker to maximize pass@k by learning from execution feedback, achieving significant improvements but requiring training data with execution labels. Valentin et al. (2025) propose incoherence as an oracle-less measure of error, detecting inconsistencies across multiple generations. Recent work has also explored uncertainty quantification for code: Sharma & David (2025) find that token-level entropy fails to correlate with code correctness unless adapted with symbolic execution-based clustering [1], while Ribeiro et al. (2025) show that standard output probabilities are poorly correlated with correctness and propose internal representation-based selection as an alternative [3]. Yang et al. (2024) demonstrate that LLM entropy effectively measures code "unnaturalness" for fault localization in automated program repair [2]. Our work complements these findings by rigorously testing whether EDIS-style entropy dynamics—a method successful for mathematical reasoning—can provide selection signals for code, and documenting the specific failure mode of entropy sparsity that limits its applicability.
annotations.summary: Related work omits 4 highly relevant recent papers on entropy/UQ for code, weakening novelty positioning and claim defensibility.

annotations.text:
3.3 NEDIS: NORMALIZED EDIS FOR CODE
We adapt EDIS to code generation by introducing two normalizations to handle variable-length sequences and entropy scale differences across problems. Our Normalized EDIS (nEDIS) is defined as:
$$
\mathbf {n E D I S} (y) = s (y) \cdot (1 + \mathbf {C V} _ {H} ^ {2})\tag{3}
$$
where $\begin{array} { r } { s ( y ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 T } ( S _ { \mathrm { b u r s t } } + S _ { \mathrm { r e b o u n d } } ) } \end{array}$ is the length-normalized spike rate and $\mathbf { C V } _ { H } = { \sigma _ { H } } / { \mu _ { H } }$ is the coefficient of variation of entropy (replacing variance to reduce scale sensitivity).
During preliminary experiments, we discovered that the original selection direction (argmin, selecting lowest instability) performed poorly for code. We hypothesize this is because code generation differs from math reasoning: longer, more complex solutions that exhibit some uncertainty may be more likely correct than short, over-confident outputs. We therefore introduce nEDIS v2:
$$
\mathrm {nEDIS\_v2} (y) = \mathrm{nEDIS} (y) \cdot T\tag{4}
$$
with argmax selection (higher score = selected). This modification multiplies by sequence length T and inverts the selection direction, fundamentally changing the method’s semantics from “low instability = reliable” to “high instability $\times \mathrm { \ l e n g t h { = } r e l i a b l e { : } }$
annotations.comment:
This section defines the nEDIS and nEDIS v2 formulas for execution-free code selection.

**Critical formula audit:** There is a significant structural issue with the nEDIS v2 definition. The nEDIS formula is:
$$\mathrm{nEDIS}(y) = s(y) \cdot (1 + CV_H^2)$$
where $s(y) = \frac{1}{2T}(S_{burst} + S_{rebound})$ is the length-normalized spike rate.

The nEDIS v2 formula then multiplies by T:
$$\mathrm{nEDIS\_v2}(y) = \mathrm{nEDIS}(y) \cdot T$$

Expanding this algebraically:
$$\mathrm{nEDIS\_v2}(y) = \frac{1}{2T}(S_{burst} + S_{rebound}) \cdot (1 + CV_H^2) \cdot T = \frac{1}{2}(S_{burst} + S_{rebound}) \cdot (1 + CV_H^2)$$

The T cancels out completely. This means nEDIS v2 is simply the un-normalized spike count times $(1 + CV_H^2)$, which is essentially the original EDIS formula with CV_H^2 replacing Var(H). The "length normalization" introduced in nEDIS is entirely undone by nEDIS v2.

**Why it matters:** The manuscript presents nEDIS as introducing "length and scale normalizations" but then immediately undoes the length normalization in v2. This creates a confusing narrative where the core innovation (normalization) is self-canceling. The manuscript should explicitly note this algebraic cancellation and explain why the v2 variant is structurally different from the intended nEDIS design. This also reinforces the later claim that nEDIS v2 captures length bias: it is essentially an un-normalized metric.

**Revision requirement:** Add one paragraph explicitly showing the algebraic cancellation and its implication. This strengthens the "optimization paradox" argument in Section 4.4.

Mentor Revised Version: (Add after Eq. 4)
Notably, expanding nEDIS v2 reveals that the length normalization is algebraically undone:
$$\mathrm{nEDIS\_v2}(y) = \frac{1}{2T}(S_{burst} + S_{rebound}) \cdot (1 + CV_H^2) \cdot T = \frac{1}{2}(S_{burst} + S_{rebound}) \cdot (1 + CV_H^2)$$
This means nEDIS v2 is structurally equivalent to the original EDIS formula with CV_H^2 replacing Var(H). The "normalization" introduced in nEDIS is completely canceled by the length multiplication in v2, suggesting that the effective selection signal comes from un-normalized spike counts rather than the length-normalized dynamics that nEDIS was designed to measure. This algebraic coincidence reinforces our later finding that nEDIS v2 likely captures length bias rather than meaningful entropy dynamics.
annotations.summary: nEDIS v2 algebraically cancels the length normalization from nEDIS, making v2 equivalent to original EDIS with CV_H^2 substitution; this structural issue must be explicitly stated.

annotations.text: Key Finding 3: nEDIS v2 improves over original nEDIS but remains inadequate. The optimized nEDIS v2 achieves +31.1pp on HumanEval and +15.0pp on MBPP compared to the original nEDIS, but still falls far short of trivial baselines.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph presents the three key findings from Table 1.

**Concrete issue:** Key Finding 3 states that "nEDIS v2 achieves +31.1pp on HumanEval and +15.0pp on MBPP compared to the original nEDIS." This delta is impressive but misleading without context. The original nEDIS achieves 25.0%/26.5% and nEDIS v2 achieves 56.1%/41.5%. The large improvement from the original to v2 is entirely due to inverting the selection direction (argmin to argmax) and multiplying by T—changes that fundamentally alter what the metric measures. Presenting this as an "improvement" risks implying that nEDIS can be optimized to work, when in fact v2 measures something entirely different from what nEDIS was designed to measure.

**Why it matters:** For a negative result paper, the framing of "optimization" is critical. If the method must be inverted to produce any signal, the original hypothesis is effectively falsified, not "optimized." The large delta reinforces the entropy sparsity argument: the original argmin selection actively selects low-confidence candidates (which in a sparse-entropy regime are the most overconfident/wrong ones).

**Revision requirement:** Reframe Key Finding 3 to explicitly state that the large improvement comes from inverting the selection direction, which falsifies the original hypothesis rather than improving the method.

Mentor Revised Version:
Key Finding 3: nEDIS v2 achieves higher scores than original nEDIS, but only by inverting the selection direction. The original nEDIS with argmin selection achieves only 25.0%/26.5% on HumanEval/MBPP—the worst among all methods. The "optimized" nEDIS v2 achieves +31.1pp on HumanEval and +15.0pp on MBPP, but this improvement comes entirely from switching to argmax selection and multiplying by sequence length, changes that fundamentally alter what the metric measures. This suggests the original hypothesis (low instability = reliable) is actively harmful for code generation, and that nEDIS v2 captures a different signal (length bias) rather than validating the entropy dynamics framework.
annotations.summary: Key Finding 3's 'improvement' narrative risks implying nEDIS is optimizable; reframe to emphasize that inverting selection direction falsifies the original hypothesis.

annotations.text:
4.3 STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE
Table 2 presents bootstrap significance tests for nEDIS v2 against each baseline. The pre-registered success criterion requires nEDIS v2 to significantly outperform both confound baselines on both benchmarks.
Pre-registered criterion NOT met. While nEDIS v2 significantly outperforms CV H on both benchmarks (p < 0.005), it fails to beat Length-only on MBPP (−24.9pp, p = 1.0). This triggers the pre-registered refutation condition: the spike-structure hypothesis does not provide selection signal beyond simple confounds.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph reports the pre-registered criterion outcome and bootstrap significance tests.

**Concrete issue:** The statistical testing protocol uses one-sided paired bootstrap with 1000 resamples, testing H1: nEDIS v2 > baseline. This is methodologically appropriate for a one-directional hypothesis. However, the experiment uses only a single model (DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct), a single set of hyperparameters (w=4, τb=1.36, τr=1.33 from the EDIS paper), and a single temperature (τ=0.8). The negative result could be specific to this particular model architecture, size, or sampling configuration rather than being a fundamental limitation of entropy dynamics for code generation.

**Why it matters:** For a negative result paper to be definitive, it should rule out alternative configurations. If nEDIS fails on DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B but might work on a base model or a different model family, the claim that "entropy dynamics do not transfer from math to code" is overgeneralized. The entropy sparsity finding (88.3% zero) is particularly model-dependent, as base models or smaller instruction-tuned models may exhibit different entropy distributions.

**Revision requirement:** Add a brief sensitivity check or explicitly bound the negative result to instruction-tuned code models of this size class. Alternatively, test nEDIS on one additional model (e.g., a base model or a different instruction-tuned model) to strengthen the generalization of the negative finding.

Mentor Revised Version:
Pre-registered criterion NOT met. While nEDIS v2 significantly outperforms CV_H on both benchmarks (p < 0.005), it fails to beat Length-only on MBPP (−24.9pp, p = 1.0). This triggers the pre-registered refutation condition: the spike-structure hypothesis does not provide selection signal beyond simple confounds. We note that this negative result is evaluated on a single instruction-tuned model (DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct) with hyperparameters carried from the original EDIS paper. While the extreme entropy sparsity (88.3% zero) is consistent with the highly calibrated behavior of modern instruction-tuned code models, we acknowledge that base models or significantly different architectures may exhibit different entropy distributions and should be tested separately.
annotations.summary: Single-model evaluation risks overgeneralizing the negative result; bound claim to instruction-tuned models or add a sensitivity check on a second model.

annotations.text: Entropy Sparsity. We find that 88.3% of per-token entropy values are exactly 0.0, indicating that the model is highly confident on most tokens. This extreme sparsity undermines spike detection: with so few non-zero entropy values, the burst and rebound patterns that EDIS relies on become noisy and unreliable. Code generation with instruction-tuned models appears fundamentally different from math reasoning in this regard.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph analyzes why entropy dynamics fail for code, focusing on entropy sparsity (88.3% zero entropy values).

**Concrete issue:** The entropy sparsity finding is a strong, novel contribution. However, the paragraph does not connect this finding to the broader literature on LLM calibration in code generation. Prior work has found that code LLMs are often poorly calibrated [1] and that token-level probabilities are not well-correlated with correctness [2]. The 88.3% zero entropy finding is a specific mechanistic explanation for why these general calibration issues prevent entropy-based methods from working.

**Why it matters:** Framing the sparsity finding as a mechanistic explanation for known calibration issues strengthens the research value. It transforms the finding from "this method fails" to "here is the specific mechanism (extreme sparsity) that explains why entropy-based methods are structurally mismatched for code generation."

**Revision requirement:** Add one sentence linking the 88.3% entropy sparsity to prior findings on code LLM miscalibration.

References:
[1] Calibration and correctness of language models for code (Spiess et al., 2024)

[2] On LLMs' Internal Representation of Code Correctness 2512.07404

Mentor Revised Version:
Entropy Sparsity. We find that 88.3% of per-token entropy values are exactly 0.0, indicating that the model is highly confident on most tokens. This extreme sparsity undermines spike detection: with so few non-zero entropy values, the burst and rebound patterns that EDIS relies on become noisy and unreliable. This finding provides a mechanistic explanation for why code LLMs are known to be poorly calibrated: when the model is maximally confident on nearly all tokens, entropy-based signals collapse to near-noise, offering no discriminative information for candidate selection. Code generation with instruction-tuned models appears fundamentally different from math reasoning in this regard, where entropy trajectories exhibit meaningful variability during exploratory problem-solving.
annotations.summary: The 88.3% sparsity finding is strong but should be linked to prior code LLM calibration literature to strengthen the mechanistic explanation.

annotations.comment:
This is the Conclusion section, summarizing the negative result, entropy sparsity, optimization paradox, and suggesting alternative approaches.

**Concrete issue:** The conclusion is concise and well-aligned with the paper's negative-result narrative. However, it does not mention the algebraic cancellation issue (nEDIS v2 undoes the length normalization) that I identified in the Method section, which is a critical structural insight that reinforces the "optimization paradox" claim. Additionally, the conclusion mentions "semantic similarity, structural analysis, or learned rankers" as alternative approaches but does not cite the recent work on internal representation-based selection (Ribeiro et al., 2025) or functional entropy (Bouchard et al., 2026), which represent the most promising concrete directions.

**Why it matters:** The conclusion should provide the strongest, most specific guidance for future work. Naming internal representations and functional equivalence as concrete alternatives (with citations) would make the paper more actionable and forward-looking.

**Revision requirement:** Add one sentence pointing to internal representation-based methods and functional entropy as promising alternative directions for execution-free code selection.

Mentor Revised Version:
We tested whether entropy dynamics can provide execution-free selection signals for code generation by adapting EDIS to nEDIS with pre-registered success criteria. Our experiments demonstrate a clear negative result: nEDIS fails the pre-registered criterion, underperforming even random first-sample selection by 12.8–27.5 percentage points. We identify entropy sparsity as a key failure mode—88.3% of entropy values are exactly zero with instruction-tuned code models, undermining spike detection. The optimization required to improve nEDIS contradicts the original hypothesis, and algebraic analysis reveals that nEDIS v2 effectively undoes the length normalization it was designed to introduce, suggesting the method captures length bias rather than meaningful entropy dynamics. This negative result prevents wasted effort on this direction and suggests that alternative approaches—such as internal representation-based selection (Ribeiro et al., 2025), functional entropy with LLM-based equivalence assessment (Bouchard et al., 2026), or learned rankers—may be needed for execution-free code selection.
annotations.summary: Conclusion should mention the algebraic cancellation insight and cite concrete alternative methods (internal representations, functional entropy) as future directions.
